facts.statement: Gastornis lived from the Paleocene to the mid-Eocene.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Paleocene – mid Eocene,

facts.statement: The genus was named after Gaston Planté, who discovered the first fossils in the Argile Plastique formation near Paris.
facts.quote: It was named after Gaston Planté, described as a "studious young man full of zeal", who had discovered the first fossils in clay (Argile Plastique) formation deposits at Meudon, near Paris.

facts.statement: Additional bones of the type species G. parisiensis were found in the mid-1860s.
facts.quote: Additional bones of the first known species, G. parisiensis, were found in the mid-1860s.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope discovered fragmentary fossils in the Wasatch Formation, New Mexico, in 1874.
facts.quote: In 1874, the American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope discovered another fragmentary set of fossils at the Wasatch Formation, New Mexico.

facts.statement: The first nearly-complete skull and skeleton were found in the Willwood Formation, Wyoming, in 1916 and described in 1917.
facts.quote: In 1916, an American Museum of Natural History expedition to the Bighorn Basin (Willwood Formation, Wyoming) found the first nearly-complete skull and skeleton, which was described in 1917 and gave scientists their first clear picture of the bird.

facts.statement: Gastornis was an extinct genus of large, flightless birds living from the middle Paleocene to the middle Eocene.
facts.quote: Gastornis is an extinct genus of large, flightless birds that lived from the middle Paleocene to the middle Eocene epochs of the Paleogene.

facts.statement: Most known fossils of Gastornis have been recovered from Europe, though species have also been reported from North America and Asia.
facts.quote: Most known fossils have been recovered from Europe, although species historically assigned to the genus have also been reported from North America and Asia.

facts.statement: Gastornis species were historically considered predators of small mammals, including early equids.
facts.quote: Gastornis species were very large birds historically considered to be predators of small mammals, including early, diminutive equids.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests Gastornis was likely herbivorous, feeding on tough plant material and seeds, rather than a predator.
facts.quote: The absence of hooked claws in known Gastornis footprints, together with analyses of its beak morphology and the isotopic signatures of its bones, suggests that it was more likely herbivorous, feeding primarily on tough plant material and seeds.

facts.statement: Gastornis is generally considered related to the Galloanserae, the clade containing modern waterfowl and gamebirds.
facts.quote: Gastornis is generally considered to be related to the Galloanserae, the clade comprising modern waterfowl and gamebirds.

facts.statement: The largest species, G. giganteus, reached about 2.15 meters in height and weighed up to 225 kilograms.
facts.quote: The largest-known species, G. giganteus would have reached about 2.15 m in maximum height, and weighed up to 175 - 225 kg in mass.

facts.statement: The skull of G. giganteus was huge and powerfully built with an extremely tall, compressed beak.
facts.quote: The skull of G. giganteus was huge compared to the body and powerfully built. The beak was extremely tall and compressed (flattened from side to side).

facts.statement: The beak of G. giganteus had a straight lip without a raptorial hook.
facts.quote: The 'lip' of the beak was straight, without a raptorial hook as found in the predatory phorusrhacids.

facts.statement: G. giganteus had a relatively short neck consisting of at least 13 massive vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebrae were short and massive, even in the neck. The neck was relatively short, consisting of at least 13 massive vertebrae.

facts.statement: G. giganteus had vestigial wings with upper wing bones small and highly reduced.
facts.quote: The wings were vestigial, with the upper wing-bones small and highly reduced, similar in proportion to the wings of the cassowary.

facts.statement: Authors have placed both European and North American birds in the order Gastornithiformes or the family Gastornithidae.
facts.quote: Following this, several authors began to recognize a greater degree of similarity between the European and North American birds, often placing both in the same order (†Gastornithiformes) or even family (†Gastornithidae).

facts.statement: A largely complete skull of G. geiselensis was described in 2024 after being discovered in 1958.
facts.quote: A largely complete skull specimen (GMH XVIII-1178-1958) of G. geiselensis was also described in 2024 after its discovery in 1958.

facts.statement: Gastornis and its relatives belong to the family Gastornithidae and were historically classified within the order Gruiformes.
facts.quote: Gastornis and its close relatives are classified together in the family Gastornithidae, and were long considered to be members of the order Gruiformes.

facts.statement: Gastornis fossils found in western and central Europe date from the late Paleocene to the early Eocene.
facts.quote: It is known from fossils found in western and central Europe, dating from the late Paleocene to the early Eocene.

facts.statement: In 2020, additional specimens from southwestern France were identified as a distinct species named G. laurenti, the most recently described Gastornis species.
facts.quote: In 2020, however, additional specimens from this location were identified as a distinct species and named G. laurenti, making them the most recently described species of Gastornis.

facts.statement: Gastornis giganteus, formerly known as Diatryma gigantea, dates from the middle Eocene of western North America.
facts.quote: Gastornis giganteus (Cope, 1876), formerly Diatryma gigantea, dates from the middle Eocene of western North America.

facts.statement: There is a long-standing debate regarding the interpretation of Gastornis's diet.
facts.quote: A long-standing debate surrounding Gastornis is the interpretation of its diet.

facts.statement: Researchers have suspected Gastornis was an ambush hunter or used pack hunting techniques to pursue prey through dense forests.
facts.quote: Consequently, Gastornis has been suspected to have been an ambush hunter and/or used pack hunting techniques to pursue or ambush prey; if Gastornis was a predator, it would have certainly needed some other means of hunting prey through the dense forest.

facts.statement: Alternatively, Gastornis could have used its strong beak to eat large or strong vegetation.
facts.quote: Alternatively, it could have used its strong beak for eating large or strong vegetation.

facts.statement: Some scientists propose that Gastornis was a carnivore that used its powerful beak to subdue prey and crack bones for marrow.
facts.quote: Some scientists have proposed that the skull of Gastornis was 'overbuilt' for a herbivorous diet and support the traditional interpretation of Gastornis as a carnivore that used its powerfully constructed beak to subdue struggling prey and crack open bones to extract marrow.

facts.statement: Footprints described in 2012 suggest gastornithids lacked strongly hooked talons, indicating a non-predatory lifestyle.
facts.quote: Footprints attributed to gastornithids (possibly a species of Gastornis itself), described in 2012, showed that these birds lacked strongly hooked talons on the hind legs, another line of evidence suggesting that they did not have a predatory lifestyle.

facts.statement: Recent studies of calcium isotopes in Gastornis bones suggest it was a true herbivore with no evidence of meat in its diet.
facts.quote: Recent evidence suggests that Gastornis was likely a true herbivore. Studies of the calcium isotopes in the bones of specimens of Gastornis by Thomas Tutken and colleagues showed no evidence that it had meat in its diet.

facts.statement: The discovery of in situ preserved gastroliths in a G. geiselensis specimen supports a herbivorous diet.
facts.quote: The first in situ preserved gastroliths in a specimen of G. geiselensis (or D. geiselensis) also conforms to its herbivorous diet.

facts.statement: Fossil eggshell fragments attributed to Gastornis have been found in Late Paleocene deposits in Spain and early Eocene deposits in France.
facts.quote: Shell fragments of huge eggs have turned up in Late Paleocene deposits of Spain and early Eocene deposits of France, namely in Provence.

facts.statement: Reconstructed Gastornis eggs measured approximately 24 by 10 cm with shells 2.3 to 2.5 mm thick.
facts.quote: Some of these fragments were complete enough to reconstruct a size of 24 by 10 cm (about 9.5 by 4 inches) with shells 2.3–2.5 mm (0.09–0.1 in) thick

facts.statement: Footprints suspected to belong to Gastornis were reported from the Paris Basin starting in 1859.
facts.quote: One set of footprints was reported from late Eocene gypsum at Montmorency and other locations of the Paris Basin in the 19th century, from 1859 onwards.

facts.statement: The largest Gastornis footprint from the Paris Basin was 40 cm long.
facts.quote: The largest of these footprints, although only consisting of a single toe's impression, was 40 cm long.

facts.statement: A controversial Gastornis footprint was found in late Eocene rocks near Black Diamond, Washington.
facts.quote: It was found in late Eocene Puget Group rocks in the Green River valley near Black Diamond, Washington.

facts.statement: At least 18 Gastornis tracks were exposed in 2009 near Bellingham, Washington, in the Eocene Chuckanut Formation.
facts.quote: In 2009, a landslide near Bellingham, Washington exposed at least 18 tracks on 15 blocks in the Eocene Chuckanut Formation.

facts.statement: The absence of raptor-like claws in Gastornis supports the hypothesis that it was a herbivore rather than a predator or scavenger.
facts.quote: Although these birds have long been considered to be predators or scavengers, the absence of raptor-like claws supports earlier suggestions that they were herbivores.

facts.statement: A single isolated feather tentatively identified as belonging to Gastornis was found in the Green River Formation.
facts.quote: A second possible Gastornis feather has since been identified, also from the Green River Formation.

facts.statement: The Gastornis-like feather measured 240 mm in length.
facts.quote: the feather measured 240 mm long and must have belonged to a gigantic bird.

facts.statement: The earliest Gastornis fossils are from the Paleocene of Europe, suggesting the genus originated there.
facts.quote: The earliest (Paleocene) fossils all come from Europe, and it is likely that the genus originated there.

facts.statement: During the Paleocene, Gastornis was the largest terrestrial tetrapod on the island continent of Europe.
facts.quote: Europe in this epoch was an island continent, and Gastornis was the largest terrestrial tetrapod of the landmass.

facts.statement: All Gastornis fossils outside of Europe date to the Eocene, but the method of dispersal remains unknown.
facts.quote: All other fossil remains are from the Eocene, though it is currently unknown how the genus Gastornis dispersed out of Europe and into other continents

facts.statement: It is debated whether Gastornis spread from Europe to North America via the Bering land bridge or via the Turgai Strait.
facts.quote: Given the possible presence of Gastornis fossils in the early Eocene of western China, these birds may have spread east from Europe and crossed into North America via the Bering land bridge.

facts.statement: The cause of Gastornis extinction is currently unclear.
facts.quote: The reason for the extinction of Gastornis is currently unclear.

facts.statement: Competition with mammals is a debated factor in Gastornis extinction, despite coexisting with mammalian megafauna herbivores.
facts.quote: Competition with mammals has often been cited as a possible factor, but in Asia and North America Gastornis occurred in faunas dominated by mammalian megafaunal herbivores like pantodonts.

facts.statement: The genus Gastornis was described by Hébert in 1855.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Hébert, 1855

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Gastornis is Gastornis parisiensis.
facts.quote: type_species: Gastornis parisiensis

facts.statement: Diatryma, Barornis, Omorhamphus, and Zhongyuanus are synonyms of Gastornis.
facts.quote: synonyms: Diatryma Cope, 1876 Barornis Marsh, 1894 Omorhamphus Sinclair, 1928 Zhongyuanus (Hou, 1980)

facts.statement: Gastornis was an extinct genus of large, flightless birds that lived during the late Paleocene and Eocene.
facts.quote: Gastornis es un género extinto de una gran ave no voladora que vivió a finales del Paleoceno y el Eoceno durante la era Cenozoica.

facts.statement: Evidence such as the lack of sharp claws and beak structure suggests Gastornis was a herbivore feeding on hard plant material and seeds.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, distintas líneas de evidencia, incluyendo la carencia de garras afiladas en las huellas conocidas de Gastornis y los estudios de la estructura de su pico, han causado que los científicos reinterpreten a estas aves como herbívoros que probablemente se alimentaban de material vegetal duro y de semillas.

facts.statement: The largest known species, G. giganteus, could reach the size of the largest moas, with a maximum height of nearly 2 meters.
facts.quote: La mayor especie conocida, G. giganteus podía alcanzar el tamaño de las mayores moas, con una altura máxima de cerca de 2 metros.

facts.statement: The skull of G. giganteus was large compared to the body and of powerful constitution.
facts.quote: El cráneo de G. giganteus era grande comparado con el cuerpo y de constitución poderosa.

facts.statement: The beak was quite high and compressed, meaning flattened on the sides.
facts.quote: El pico era bastante alto y comprimido (es decir, aplanado por los lados).

facts.statement: The "lip" of the beak was straight, lacking a hook at the end seen in birds of prey and terror birds.
facts.quote: El "labio" del pico era recto, sin un gancho al final como el que se ve en las aves de presa y las forusrácidas.

facts.statement: The nostrils were small and practically positioned in front of the eyes, halfway along the skull.
facts.quote: Las narinas eran pequeñas y prácticamente posicionadas en frente de los ojos, a mitad del cráneo.

facts.statement: The neck was relatively short, consisting of at least 13 of these large vertebrae.
facts.quote: El cuello era relativamente corto, consistente en al menos unas 13 de estas grandes vértebras.

facts.statement: The wings were vestigial, with the upper wing bones being small and extremely reduced, similar in proportion to those of the cassowary.
facts.quote: Las alas eran vestigiales, siendo los huesos superiores del ala pequeños y sumamente reducidos, similares en proporción a los de las alas del casuario.

facts.statement: Gastornis was originally described in 1855 from a fragmentary skeleton.
facts.quote: Gastornis fue descrito originalmente en 1855 a partir de un esqueleto fragmentario.

facts.statement: It was named in honor of Gaston Planté, described as a "young scholar full of enthusiasm", who had discovered the first fossils in the deposits of the Argile Plastique formation in Meudon, near Paris.
facts.quote: Fue nombrado en honor de Gaston Planté, descrito como un "joven estudioso lleno de entusiasmo", quien había descubierto los primeros fósiles en los depósitos de la formación Argile Plastique en Meudon, cerca de París.

facts.statement: In 1874, American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope discovered another fragmentary collection of fossils in the Wasatch Formation of New Mexico, USA.
facts.quote: En el año 1874, el paleontólogo estadounidense Edward Drinker Cope descubrió otra colección fragmentaria de fósiles en la Formación Wasatch de Nuevo México, Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: Gastornis and its closest relatives were classified in the family Gastornithidae and were long considered members of the order Gruiformes.
facts.quote: Gastornis y sus parientes más cercanos fueron clasificados en la familia Gastornithidae, y fueron durante mucho tiempo considerados como miembros del orden Gruiformes.

facts.statement: Starting in the late 1980s with the first phylogenetic analysis of gastornithid relationships, a consensus grew that these birds were close relatives of the lineage including ducks and chajás, the Anseriformes.
facts.quote: Iniciando a fines de los años 1980 con el primer análisis filogenético de las relaciones de las gastornítidas, comenzó a crecer el consenso de que estas aves eran parientes cercanas del linaje que incluye a los patos y los chajás, los Anseriformes.

facts.statement: A 2007 study showed that gastornithids were a branch that separated early from the anseriforms and formed the sister group to all other members of that lineage.
facts.quote: Un estudio de 2007 mostró que los gastornítidos eran una rama que se separó tempranamente de los anseriformes, y formaba el grupo hermano de todos los demás miembros de ese linaje.

facts.statement: Gastornithids are sometimes included in their own biological order, Gastornithiformes.
facts.quote: Los gastornítidos son a veces incluidos en su propio orden biológico, Gastornithiformes.

facts.statement: The time range is from the Selandian to the Ypresian, between 61.66 and 48.07 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Selandian to Ypresian (61.66 to 48.07 million years ago)

facts.statement: Upon recognizing the apparently close relationship between gastornithids and anseriforms, some researchers classified them within the anseriform group itself, while others restricted the term Anseriformes to the crown group of all modern species and named the larger group including extinct anseriform relatives, such as gastornithids, Anserimorphae.
facts.quote: Al reconocerse la aparentemente cercana relación entre los gastornítidos y los anseriformes, algunos investigadores los clasificaron dentro del grupo de los anseriformes en sí. Otros restringieron el uso del término Anseriformes solo al grupo corona formado por todas las especies modernas, y denominaron al grupo mayor que incluye a los parientes extintos de los anseriformes, como los gastornítidos, con el nombre Anserimorphae.
